1:
The chapter opens with the sealing of a solemn covenant, and the witnesses set the whole act in view before they trace a single name. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks the change in the manner of covenanting: when Israel was first brought into covenant with God at Sinai it was done by sacrifice and the sprinkling of blood, as at Exodus 24:8; but here it was done by the more natural and common way of sealing and subscribing the written articles, which bound the people to no more than was already their duty. The heads of the congregation set their hands and seals as its representatives, since it would have been an endless work for every private person to do it, and their example would tell upon all the rest.

The reformed John Gill notes simply that those who sealed were the persons whose names follow, while the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws out the sense of it: they subscribed both in their own names and in the name of all the rest. Henry orders the four ranks that Adam Clarke also lays down — Nehemiah the governor signed first, to show his forwardness and set others a good example, for those above others in dignity should go before them in the way of God; next twenty-two priests; then seventeen Levites, among whom stood most of those who had been the mouth of the congregation in the prayer of Nehemiah 9:4-5; and last forty-four of the chief of the people, who subscribed for themselves and all the rest.

The witnesses share a common puzzle: the absence of Ezra. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke wonders that among all these we hear nothing of Ezra, nor of the high priest Eliashib, nor of any prophet, though some must have been at Jerusalem; Wesley supposes Ezra was kept away by sickness or some extraordinary impediment, for we meet him again at the dedication of the wall in Nehemiah 12:36. Henry offers the gentler thought that Ezra, having already done his part as a scribe at the reading of the law in Nehemiah 8:2, now left it to others to do theirs. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds a note on the first name after the governor, taking Zidkijah to be Zadok the scribe, Nehemiah's secretary, named at Nehemiah 13:13 and compared with Ezra 4:8. The voices do not divide; together they frame the sealed covenant as a written, representative, and public renewal of an old obligation, undertaken by the leaders that the whole people might be drawn after them into fresh loyalty to God.
28:
Having named the leaders who sealed, the record turns to the whole body of the people who joined them, and the witnesses weigh who exactly is gathered in. The reformed John Gill takes "the rest of the people" to be those who did not themselves sign and seal the document, yet were no less parties to the covenant. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke makes the point explicit: all the people had, in one or other of the classes that sealed — priests, Levites, or chiefs — their representatives, and by that representative sealing they held themselves as truly bound as if each had set his own hand to the parchment.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott dwells on the striking clause "all they that had separated themselves from the people of the lands unto the law of God." Were these proselytes from heathenism, he says, the verse would be a perfect description of the constituents of the people; but there is as yet no record of a recognised body of such converts, and the word "separated" is the same that appears with another sense at Nehemiah 9:2. Moreover the verses that follow bear specially in mind the danger to God's law arising out of commerce with the heathen, so that the separated are more likely the descendants of Israelites who had remained in the land and now joined the returned community. The added words "every one having knowledge and having understanding," Ellicott notes, take in the children who were old enough to enter intelligently into the oath.

The witnesses gather the verse into a picture of a covenant that reached every rank and age. Not the nobles only, nor the ministering orders, but the porters and the singers and the Nethinim, the wives and the sons and the daughters, all who had years enough to know what they did, are drawn into the bond. Gill's note that these were the unsealed multitude, Clarke's that they were bound through their representatives, and Ellicott's that even the discerning children were included, together render the sweep of it: the whole people, high and low, native and newly joined, old enough to understand, made themselves one in the engagement their leaders had sealed. A covenant undertaken by heads of houses is here owned by the households themselves, so that none might afterward plead that the pledge was not his own; and the very naming of wives and children shows how the reformation was meant to reach into every home in the land, and not to stop at the doors of the great.
29:
The verse names the act by which the people made the covenant their own — "they clave to their brethren, their nobles, and entered into a curse, and into an oath" — and the witnesses gather around both the cleaving and the swearing. The reformed John Gill reads the cleaving as a public declaration of assent: the commonalty attended to what their nobles had sealed, approved it, and ratified in their own persons what had been done in their name. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the participle "holding with," and take "the rest of the people" to be the members of the community apart from the princes and heads of the priestly and Levitical orders; the Nethinim, they add, were probably represented by the heads of the Levites, and the separated ones are the descendants of Israelites left in the land, now joined to the new community, parted from the heathen unto the law of God that they might live according to it.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley lingers on the nobles and the honour done them. The commonalty agreed with their nobles in this good work; great men never look so great, he says, as when they encourage religion and are examples of it, and by that, more than by anything, they win an interest in the most valuable of their inferiors, who will cleave to them the closer. Observe, he adds, that the nobles are called the people's brethren, for in the things of God rich and poor, high and low, meet together; and the people cleaving to them means that they ratified what the others had done in their names. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke makes the same point of the unsealed: though they did not sign the instrument, they bound themselves under a solemn oath to fulfil its conditions and to walk according to the law of Moses.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott weighs the two solemn words. It was a union of the people as such, sprung from a deep national conviction; and they entered into "a curse and an oath" — the oath assuming the obligation, the curse imprecating the penalty of its violation, as in the covenant of Deuteronomy 29:12. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Clarke fix the ratifying assent of those who had not sealed, Keil and Delitzsch the classes and the newly joined who held with their brethren, Wesley the brotherhood of noble and commoner in the work of God, and Ellicott the binding force of an oath sealed under a self-invoked curse. Together they show a whole people willingly fastening upon themselves, by the most sacred of bonds, the duty to keep all the commandments of the Lord their God.
30:
The first particular article of the covenant is against mixed marriage — "that we would not give our daughters unto the people of the land, nor take their daughters for our sons" — and the witnesses read it as the reform striking first at the sin that had done the most damage. The reformed John Gill notes that the people had been guilty of this very thing and were prone to it still, intermarrying with the surrounding nations as they had done before, the guilt owned already at Ezra 9:2. The pledge, that is, is aimed at a known and besetting fault, the door through which idolatry had always entered Israel.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set this article at the head of the covenant's several engagements, which run on through the sabbath, the seventh year, and the dues of the temple. If the community seriously meant to walk by the rule of God's law, they must first shut the way to the heathen alliances that had corrupted them; and so the very first clause the people bind themselves to is the refusal of marriage with the people of the land. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke puts the sense in a phrase: to give no daughters and take none is to "make no affinity with the people of the land" — to renounce the kinship and the compromise that such marriages brought.

The witnesses feel the wisdom of beginning the reform just here. In our covenants with God, the point runs, we should engage most particularly against the sins we have most often been overtaken by; and Israel's history had proved marriage with the heathen to be exactly such a sin, the standing occasion of her apostasy. Gill's reminder that they had already fallen into it, Keil and Delitzsch's placing of it first among the covenant's terms, and Clarke's blunt gloss that it meant making no affinity at all, together mark the seriousness of the pledge. The people do not vow in the abstract to keep the law; they name the concrete temptation and bar it, resolving that the holy seed should not again be mingled with the peoples whose gods had so often drawn Israel away. It is the mark of true repentance, the witnesses imply, to strike first and hardest at the sin that has hurt one most, and to fence it about with a solemn engagement before God, that the household of faith be not opened again to the very corruption from which it had just been so dearly recovered.
31:
The covenant's second and third articles concern the sabbath and the sabbatical year — "if the people of the land bring ware... on the sabbath day to sell, that we would not buy it," and "that we would leave the seventh year, and the exaction of every debt." The reformed John Gill glosses the "ware" as any goods brought to be sold, which, being bought, might be carried away; the pledge is not to trade on the holy day even with the heathen who kept no sabbath. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gathers both vows into one resolve: "we will most solemnly keep the Sabbath," and "we will let the land have its Sabbath, and rest every seventh year," pointing back to the law of the land's rest in Exodus 23:10-11.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott refines each clause. "Or on the holy day" extends the rule to the great festivals equally with the weekly sabbaths of rest; "leave the seventh year" means that in it the ground should be left untilled; and "the exaction of every debt" is the Lord's release of the seventh year commanded in Deuteronomy 15:2, when the creditor was to loose his hold on what was owed. The people bind themselves, that is, not only to a day but to a whole rhythm of rest and release that touched their fields, their markets, and their debtors.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley presses the spiritual root of the sabbath clause. The "people of the land" are the heathen, whose wares the covenanters would not buy; and they who covenant to keep all the commandments of God must particularly covenant to keep the sabbath holy, for the profanation of that day, he warns, is a sure inlet to all manner of profaneness. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the plain sense of refusing sabbath trade, Clarke and Ellicott the double vow of the weekly rest and the seventh-year release, and Wesley the reason the sabbath is singled out — that letting it slip opens the way to every other neglect. It is telling to the witnesses that a people just recovered from captivity should fence the sabbath and the sabbatical year with special care, for it was for the long neglect of the land's rest that God had made it keep its sabbaths through the years of exile, and they would not again forfeit their place by grasping after gain on the days that were the Lord's. What had helped bring on the captivity they now bind themselves to reverse.
32:
The covenant now passes from things forbidden to duties resumed, and the first is a self-imposed tax for the temple — "to charge ourselves yearly with the third part of a shekel for the service of the house of our God." The reformed John Gill notes that they made an ordinance for themselves, binding themselves by their own act to a thing the written law had not in so many words required of them. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry seizes the turn: having covenanted against the sins they had been guilty of, they now oblige themselves to revive the duties they had neglected, for we must not only cease to do evil but learn to do well. A stock had to be raised for the furnishing of God's table and altar; there was no rich king now, as Hezekiah had been, to provide the shewbread and the daily lambs, and the priests could not bear the charge, and so the people agreed to contribute yearly, every one of them, this small sum — about ten pence apiece — that when every one gave, though but little, the whole might come to a considerable supply.

Over the amount the witnesses raise the obvious question, for the law of Exodus 30:13 had fixed the ransom of every soul at half a shekel. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke answers from their poverty: the general want that their wars and captivity had brought made it impossible to give more, and since the poor and the rich were to give alike, the sum was lowered to what the poorest could meet; yet when the people grew more prosperous the half shekel was resumed, as the didrachma demanded in Matthew 17:24 shows, the very tax our Lord paid with the stater from the fish's mouth.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the verse the same way: here is the origin of that annual rate for the general service of the temple which was afterwards raised to a half shekel, the more ancient half shekel of the law having been only an occasional tax. The witnesses converge on the willingness of it, which Henry most admires. The Tirshatha did not impose this charge from above; the people made it an ordinance for themselves and charged themselves with it, and let no people expect the blessing of God, Henry warns, who will not make conscience of maintaining his public worship. It goes well with our own houses, he adds, when care is taken that the work of God's house go well; and here a poor people, taxing themselves a third of a shekel out of their want, showed the very temper that draws down heaven's favour — every hand giving its little, and the little made much by the giving of all.
33:
The verse itemizes what the yearly third-shekel was to furnish — "the shewbread, and the continual meat offering, and the continual burnt offering, of the sabbaths, of the new moons, for the set feasts... and for the sin offerings to make an atonement for Israel." The reformed John Gill reads it as the defraying of a constant expense, beginning with the twelve loaves of shewbread set week by week upon the holy table. The whole round of the sanctuary's service, from the daily offering to the sin-offerings of atonement, had to be paid for, and the people's self-imposed levy was the fund appointed to meet it.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the sense of the charge. "We ordained for ourselves," they render — literally, we laid upon ourselves — the third of a shekel yearly for the service of the house of God; the text does not name who was bound to pay it, taking that for a known custom, but the payment is plainly a revival of the Mosaic precept of Exodus 30:13, that every man of twenty years and upward should give his tribute to the Lord, a tax still paid in Christ's day as Matthew 17:24 attests, though here lowered to a third in view of the community's poverty. They reject the notion of Aben Ezra that a third was to be paid over and above the legal half, and insist that "the service of the house of God" here means not the building or repair of the temple but the regular worship carried on within it.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry supplies the pastoral weight the list carries. It was a constant charge, he observes, to provide shewbread for the table, two lambs for the daily offerings and four for the sabbaths, with more and costlier sacrifices for the other feasts, besides the occasional sin-offerings and meat-offerings and drink-offerings; and where there was no settled fund the service must languish. Let not any people expect the blessing of God, Henry urges, unless they make conscience of keeping up the public worship of him, for the work of God's house is likely to go on well only when care is taken to supply it. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch fix the objects of the fund and the law it revived, and Henry draws the lesson that a worship worth keeping is worth paying for — that a people who would have God's ordinances continued among them must be content to bear the cost of them, and count it no burden but a privilege to furnish the table of the Lord.
34:
The covenant provides next for the fuel of the altar — "we cast the lots among the priests, the Levites, and the people for the wood offering, to bring it into the house of our God... to burn upon the altar." The reformed John Gill notes the manner of the casting: the priests and Levites were in one lot and the people in another, as Aben Ezra observed, so that each division should know its appointed turn. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch explain the need for such an arrangement: the law of Leviticus 6:12 required that fire be kept always burning on the altar and that the priest burn wood on it every morning, yet it gave no directions for procuring the wood; the rulers of the people must therefore provide for its regular delivery, and the lot fixed which houses should bring it and when.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sets the custom in its history. There was no wood-offering under the law properly so called; the providing of fuel had been the business of the Nethinim, the hewers of wood and drawers of water to the congregation, but after the captivity few of these were to be found, most having chosen to remain in the land of their exile. Since there were not enough to supply the altar, the people now cast lots — not who should furnish the wood, but which district should bring it at a given season of the year — that there might be a constant supply; and in time, Clarke notes, this bringing of the wood grew into a great day and was made a feast, the Xylophoria of which Josephus writes, though it is named nowhere in Scripture.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the verse to the same end. "As it is written in the law" points to the standing fire of Leviticus 6:12, which the wood was to feed; and here, he says, is the origin of the feast of the wood-offering, a special day afterwards substituted for the "times appointed year by year," the lot determining the order in which the several classes should supply the fuel. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the division of the lot, Keil and Delitzsch the gap in the law that made human provision necessary, Clarke the decay of the Nethinim that threw the duty upon the whole people, and Ellicott the later feast it became. Together they show a people so in earnest for the worship of God that they would not leave even the firewood of the altar to chance, but ordered by lot that the sacred fire should never want fuel — the humblest service of the house made a matter of solemn covenant and equal turns.
35:
The covenant turns to the firstfruits — "to bring the firstfruits of our ground, and the firstfruits of all fruit of all trees, year by year, unto the house of the LORD." The reformed John Gill is careful to distinguish this article from the one before: they did not cast lots to bring the firstfruits, as they had for the wood, but bound themselves by oath, according to the law, to render them; and he notes that Aben Ezra would restrict the firstfruits here to the sheaf of the firstfruits and the two wave-loaves, though the broader sense takes in the first of all the fruits of the earth.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the clause as following straight upon the "we made ordinances" of the covenant's opening, and observes how the several firstfruits are specified exactly according to the Mosaic law, which had made this natural expression of piety an obligation. The very minuteness of the specification, he adds, is significant: it implies that neglect had crept in, and that the duty had to be spelled out again in detail because it had been let slip. A people returning to God does not merely renew the general principle but names each particular that had been forgotten, that nothing might again be quietly dropped.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the firstfruits and the tithes that follow into a single resolve to maintain the ministers of the house, that they might mind their work and not be forced to neglect it in making provision for their families. The work of God's house is likely to go on, he says, when those who serve at the altar can live, and live comfortably, upon the altar; and firstfruits and tithes were then the chief branches of the ministers' revenue. It was for the withholding of these very dues that God, by the prophet, had charged the people with robbing him in Malachi 3:8, promising, if they would bring the tithes into the storehouse, to pour out a blessing upon them. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the firstfruits as a matter of sworn duty and not of lot, Ellicott the careful naming of each kind as a sign of former neglect, and Henry the end the whole served — the support of God's ministers and the keeping-up of his worship. Together they show a people binding themselves to give God the first and best of field and orchard, owning by that offering that the increase was his gift and the ministers of his house their charge to maintain.
36:
The offering of the firstborn follows the firstfruits — "also the firstborn of our sons, and of our cattle... and the firstlings of our herds and of our flocks, to bring to the house of our God, unto the priests." The reformed John Gill distinguishes the two sorts named: the firstborn of their sons and of their unclean cattle, such as the ass, were to be redeemed by a price paid to the priests, while the clean firstlings were brought for sacrifice, all as it is written in the law. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch trace each item to its statute — the firstfruits of the ground to Exodus 23:19, the firstfruits of the trees to Numbers 18:13, the redemption of the firstborn sons to Numbers 18:16, and the firstlings of herd and flock, whose fat was consumed on the altar and whose flesh fell to the priests, to Numbers 18:17.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke points to the ground of the whole law of the firstborn in Exodus 13:2: the Lord had a right to all the firstborn, but instead of them he was pleased to take the tribe of Levi, so that the Levites served at the tabernacle and temple in the room of the firstborn of all the tribes. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the distinction Gill had drawn: the firstborn of the sons and the unclean cattle were, with a money valuation, to be redeemed according to the priests' estimate, while the firstlings of the herds and flocks were brought to the priests that minister for sacrifice — the one class ransomed, the other offered.

The witnesses do not divide, and their patient tracing of each clause to its law is itself a testimony to the temper of the covenant. Israel is not inventing new burdens but resuming old and forgotten dues, binding herself again to the whole round of firstfruits and firstlings by which she confessed that the first and best of children, crops, and cattle belonged to the God who gave them. Gill and Ellicott mark the double treatment of the firstborn — redeemed where the creature was unclean or the child a son, offered where the beast was fit for the altar; Keil and Delitzsch anchor every particular in the Mosaic text; and Clarke recalls the deep reason of it, that the Levites stood before God as the ransom of Israel's firstborn. Together they show a people renewing, item by item, the acknowledgment that their increase was not their own but held in trust from the Lord, whose claim upon the firstborn ran back to the night he spared them in Egypt and took them for his own.
37:
The covenant reaches the tithes and the first of the dough — "the firstfruits of our dough, and our offerings, and the fruit of all manner of trees, of wine and of oil, unto the priests... and the tithes of our ground unto the Levites." The reformed John Gill notes that the firstfruits of the dough were to be brought according to the law that appointed them, a cake of the first of the kneaded meal set apart for the priest. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch lay out the whole flow of the dues: the firstfruits of dough and the heave-offerings and the fruit of the trees, with the wine and the oil, were to be brought to the priests, to the chambers of the house of God, while the tithes of the ground went to the Levites, who were to gather them in the country towns, the cities of their tillage.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends to those store-chambers and to the country places named. "The chambers of the house of our God" are the store-rooms of the temple, described of old at the first building in 1 Kings 6, to which Hezekiah had once added a treasure-house for the tithes, as 2 Chronicles 31:11 records; and "the cities of our tillage" are the agricultural towns, so called from the fruits of the earth that were first gathered there before being carried up to Jerusalem. The tithe, that is, was collected where it grew and then brought in to the central chambers, that the ministers of the house might have their portion ready to hand.

The witnesses read the arrangement as a careful provision for those who had no inheritance of their own. The Levites, scattered through the towns, were to receive the tithe of the land in the very places where the people dwelt; the priests, at the temple, were to have the firstfruits and the heave-offerings in their chambers. Gill fixes the first of the dough as a matter of standing law, Keil and Delitzsch the distribution of the several dues between priest and Levite, and Ellicott the store-chambers and the country towns where the reckoning was made. Together they show a people binding themselves to feed the whole ministering household of God — not the priests only at the altar, but the Levites in the outlying cities — that none who served the sanctuary might be left to want, and that the worship of the house might be sustained by a settled and orderly supply drawn from every field in the land.
38:
The verse guards the tithe with a check — "the priest the son of Aaron shall be with the Levites, when the Levites take tithes: and the Levites shall bring up the tithe of the tithes unto the house of our God." The reformed John Gill reads it as a safeguard of trust: a priest was always to be present with the Levites when they received the tithes, that they might not be under any temptation, nor lie under any suspicion, of defrauding the priests of the portion due to them out of what was gathered. The presence of the son of Aaron was a witness that the reckoning was honest and the priests' share duly set aside.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke explains the "tithe of the tithes." The tithes of all the produce of the fields were brought to the Levites, and out of these the Levites gave a tenth part to the priests; this tenth of the tenth is what the verse calls the tithe of the tithes, and the law for it stands in Numbers 18:26. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sends the reader to the same passage for the reason of the sharp distinction the verse draws between the priest, the son of Aaron, and the Levites, the children of Levi: a priest was present when the tithes were gathered in the Levitical cities, to secure the tithe of the tithe, which the Levites then carried up to Jerusalem.

The witnesses do not divide, and they find in this small provision a wise care against the abuses that beset even holy things. Where money and produce pass through many hands there is room for suspicion and for fraud, and the covenant forestalls both by requiring a priest at the Levites' side when the tithe is taken, so that the giving of the tenth to the priests should be open and above reproach. Gill fixes the guarding of the priests' due, Clarke the arithmetic of the tenth drawn from the tenth, and Ellicott the presence of the son of Aaron in the country cities where the tithe was gathered. Together they show a reformation attentive not only to the great matters of marriage and sabbath but to the honest handling of the sanctuary's revenue — a people resolved that the maintenance of God's ministers should be managed as uprightly as it was given freely, and that no shadow of dishonesty should fall upon the offerings brought to the house of God.
39:
The covenant closes on a great resolve — "we will not forsake the house of our God." The reformed John Gill reads the opening clause as the sum of all the foregoing dues: the children of Israel and the children of Levi were to bring the offering of the corn, the new wine, and the oil unto the chambers of the temple, where the vessels of the sanctuary and the ministering priests and porters and singers were. All the particular tithes and firstfruits already named are gathered here into one steady stream flowing toward the house, and crowned with the pledge never to abandon it.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fastens on that closing pledge and swells it into a meditation. Here was a glorious resolution, he says, and had they been faithful to it they had been a great and good people to this day. The Church of God is the house of God, where he keeps his constant dwelling; true believers are his family within it; the ministers of the word are its officers; the worship of God is its grand employment, and his ordinances the food that sustains its members. Those who do not forsake the house of their God, Clarke presses, are they who continue in the faith, who grow in grace, who labour and bring forth fruit, who conscientiously attend all the ordinances, and who take care that the offerings of the house be duly made, providing for those who labour in the word and doctrine.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds the sober historical note. "Shall bring" marks that the priests themselves were exempted from the toil of gathering the tithes, which was laid upon the Levites and the people; and the pledge "we will not forsake the house of our God," he observes, is explained both in its making and in its breaking by Nehemiah 13:11-14, where Nehemiah, returning, found the chambers emptied and the Levites fled to their fields for want of their portion, and had to contend with the rulers, "Why is the house of God forsaken?" The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the offerings flowing to the chambers, Clarke the height of the vow and all it embraced, and Ellicott the grief of its later failure. Together they leave the covenant where it ends, on the noblest of its promises and the shadow of its coming breach: a people vowing, with firstfruits and tithes and their whole heart, never to leave the worship of God to starve — a vow so soon forgotten that it had to be pressed upon them again, and yet a vow that stands as the true crown and aim of all the rest, for to forsake the house of God is, as Clarke says, to forsake God himself.
2:
With the governor's name set down, the register turns to the priests, and the first of them is Seraiah. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch pause here over the nature of the document itself, for this verse opens the roll of those who set their seal to it. Upon all that had gone before — the day of prayer and fasting and the great confession of Nehemiah 9 — the assembled people made what the Hebrew calls an amanah, a firm and sure agreement, and committed it to writing, that so solemn a day might leave a lasting mark. They weigh the disputed phrase "because of all this," rejecting the readings that take it as "after all this" or "in all this evil that had befallen us," and fixing it rather as "upon all this" — that is, upon the foundation of the preceding penitence the covenant was built. The princes, the Levites, and the priests signed the sealed document, binding themselves by oath to separate from the heathen and to keep the commandments of God.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends to the name that heads the priestly list. Seraiah, he explains, is not a private person but the family name of the high-priestly house to which both Ezra and Eliashib belonged; and it was one of that house, probably Ezra himself, who affixed its seal on behalf of the whole line. Thus the very first priestly signature is a house rather than a man, the ancient sacerdotal family standing as one and pledging itself in a single name to the renewed covenant.

The witnesses converge on the weight of what this sealing meant. The document was no light memorandum but a written and witnessed bond, sealed by the heads of the houses that all the people might be held to it; and that the priests should be named directly after the governor marks the order of the whole chapter, in which those nearest to holy things are called first to bind themselves to the law they were set to guard. Keil and Delitzsch note that the same word for this settled agreement recurs later in the book at Nehemiah 11:23, where a sure ordinance is again in view; and Ellicott's identification of Seraiah with the high-priestly stock shows how the register, for all its bare look, is a careful record of representative men and families, each seal standing for many. What the people had wept over and confessed they now, through their leaders, subscribed and sealed, that the covenant might outlast the emotion that gave it birth, and bind the generation to come as firmly as the one that signed.
3:
The priestly roll runs on — Pashur, Amariah, Malchijah — and the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch treat the whole company of sealing priests together, some one-and-twenty names in all before the list closes with "these were the priests." These, they observe, are the courses of the priesthood that had returned from Babylon, set down here as the heads of their houses, each name standing not for a single man only but for the order he represented. The historian, they note, keeps them in their ranks, comparing the roll with the register of the returning priests in Ezra 2:36 and following, so that the record of who bound himself to the covenant might be full and exact.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry had numbered these priests at twenty-two and drew a lesson from their place at the head of the list: next to Nehemiah the governor they subscribed, and it was fitting that those whose office was to teach the law should be foremost in binding themselves to keep it, their example telling upon all the rest. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke likewise reckons the priests the second of the four classes that sealed, filling the verses from the second to the eighth; and he marvels, as the other witnesses do, that among so many priestly names neither Ezra the scribe nor the high priest Eliashib should appear. That the register should open with the sacred orders is, to the witnesses, no accident but a token that reformation must begin at the sanctuary, with the men set apart to guard the holiness of Israel.

The witnesses do not divide over these bare names, and their very restraint is instructive. Pashur and Amariah and Malchijah are not men whose deeds fill the history; their one recorded act is that, as heads of their fathers' houses, they set their seal to a written covenant to walk in God's law. Keil and Delitzsch's care to trace such names to the returning courses, and Henry's insistence that the priests led the way, together render the register something more than a list: it is the muster-roll of a penitent nation's leaders, the priests first among them, pledging by seal and signature the obedience they had so long neglected. Each name, obscure as it now sounds, was a public and deliberate committal, that the people who followed might see their teachers bound before them and be drawn to bind themselves; for a reform led from the altar is likely to reach the whole camp, and a priesthood that pledges first has earned the right to call the people after it.
11:
The Levitical roll runs on with Micha, Rehob, and Hashabiah, and the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch treat them within the company of some fourteen Levites who sealed, the brethren of Jeshua, Binnui, and Kadmiel. These, they hold, are to be regarded as heads of Levitical houses; and having closed the Levites the register passes at once to the chief of the people, whom Keil and Delitzsch number at forty-four names, thirteen of them found in the list of the kindreds that returned with Zerubbabel in Ezra 2. The greater number here than there they explain by the growth of the houses over the years, several heads subscribing where once a single kindred stood, with fresh accessions besides.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms that several Levitical family names are traceable in the earlier lists of the return, so that the men sealing here are of the old serving stock. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, reckoning the Levites at seventeen, repeats the point that most of those who had been the mouth of the congregation in the prayer of Nehemiah 9:4-5 are found among these subscribers; those who lead in prayer, he says, should lead in every other good work, and here they did, not laying upon others the burdens they declined to touch.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps these names in the third of the four sealing classes, the Levites between the priests and the chief of the people. The witnesses do not divide over Micha and Rehob and Hashabiah. What they draw from the list is the same lesson that governs the whole register: these are representative men, heads of houses, binding by their seal not themselves only but the families they led. That the roll should keep even such obscure names, and that Keil and Delitzsch should trace the small discrepancy of number to the honest growth of the community, marks the record as a careful and faithful one. The Levites who had carried Israel's worship and voiced her confession now stand named among those who pledged her amendment; and the register moves in due order from the ministers of the house to the leaders of the laity, that the covenant might be seen to gather every rank of the people into one solemn engagement to keep the law of God, none excusing himself because his name was small. Micha and Rehob and Hashabiah are but names to us now, yet each was a house pledged, and the worship they served by day they here bound themselves and their sons to guard by covenant.
16:
The lay roll runs on with Adonijah, Bigvai, and Adin, and the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep them among the forty-four heads of the people whose names fill the register down to Baanah. These, they repeat, are partly the ancient kindreds of the return and partly the newer houses grown out of them, together with the elders of the lesser towns of Judah and Benjamin; and they note that when the list of names is done, the record turns to declare how all the rest of the community — the priests, the Levites, the porters, the singers, the Nethinim, and the people — acceded to the agreement thus signed by the princes and the heads of the orders, binding themselves by oath to walk in God's law.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott's rule holds here too: some of these names are personal, some familial, and some local, the whole bearing witness that the houses had multiplied since the days of Ezra 2. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry observes that many of those named in the register of Nehemiah 7:8 as heads of houses reappear here among the chief of the people who sealed, the current head bearing the ancestral name and subscribing for all his father's house; their names, he adds, are set on record to their honour as men active in reviving religion, and the memory of such shall be blessed.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps these within the fourth sealing class, the chief of the people, which runs from the fourteenth verse to the twenty-seventh. The witnesses do not divide over Adonijah and Bigvai and Adin. What they press is the representative and gathering character of the whole roll: these heads sealed for their houses, and behind the sealed names stood the unsealed multitude who, as the record will presently say, clave to their brethren and entered by oath into the same covenant. Keil and Delitzsch's noting that the list of names opens at once into the accession of all the people shows how the register was meant to be read — not as an end in itself but as the roll of leaders through whom a whole nation bound itself to God. Henry's honour and Clarke's ordering meet in the same truth: the chief men subscribed that the people might follow, and the covenant sealed by the few was owned by the all. Adonijah and Bigvai and Adin are dim names on an ancient roll, yet each carried a household into the bond, and the register preserves them that the breadth of the pledge, and the honour of those who led it, might not be lost.
8:
The priestly roll is here rounded off — Maaziah, Bilgai, Shemaiah — with the closing note, "these were the priests." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads that summary as a heading for the whole company just named, the names of the priestly families rather than of chance individuals, to be set beside the register of the returning priests in Nehemiah 12:1-6. With this line the first of the four sealing classes is complete, and the record can pass to the Levites.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, surveying the priestly list as a whole, count these among the one-and-twenty names that stand before the summary, each a head of one of the courses that had come up from Babylon and now sealed the covenant for his house. The historian's care to close the priestly names with a plain "these were the priests," they imply, is of a piece with his method throughout the register, keeping the orders distinct and marking where one class ends and the next begins, that the roll might be read without confusion.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke together weigh the significance of a priestly list so full. Henry numbers the priests at twenty-two and sets them next after the governor, as was fitting for the men whose office was to teach the law; Clarke counts the same class through these verses and joins the standing wonder of the chapter, that neither Ezra nor the high priest Eliashib is found among them. The witnesses do not divide. What they draw from the closing of the priestly roll is the seriousness with which the sacred order bound itself. Maaziah and Bilgai and Shemaiah are no more than names to us now, yet each was the seal of a priestly house pledged to the covenant, and their being gathered under the words "these were the priests" marks the completeness of the sacerdotal committal. That the reformation of Israel should open with the whole body of the priests subscribing, house by house, to walk in God's law is to the witnesses a hopeful sign; for when the teachers of a people lead in returning to God, the people are the likelier to follow, and the register that begins at the altar is well begun, and promises well for all that is to be built upon it. The men who ministered atonement for others here own before all Israel that they too must keep the covenant they urge, and their seal at the head of the roll is the first stone of the whole reform.
9:
The register crosses from the priests to the Levites — "and the Levites: both Jeshua the son of Azaniah, Binnui of the sons of Henadad, Kadmiel." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that of these Levitical family names several are traceable in the earlier records of the return, at Ezra 2:40 and its parallels, so that the Levites sealing here are of the same houses that had first come up to serve the restored altar. The three names that open the list — Jeshua, Binnui, and Kadmiel — are the heads under whom the Levitical company is gathered.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fill in the reckoning: the Levites who sealed number some fourteen, led by these three and their brethren; the sons of Jeshua and Kadmiel had returned with seventy-four other Levites under Zerubbabel, and Jeshua, Binnui, and Kadmiel appear again as heads of Levitical orders in Nehemiah 12:8. The rest, of whom little is known, are to be taken as heads of Levitical houses, each sealing for the family he led. Thus the second rank of the temple's ministers is bound to the covenant in the persons of its chief men.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out what made the Levites' subscription especially fitting. Reckoning them at seventeen, he observes that among them stood most of those who had been the mouth of the congregation in the great prayer of Nehemiah 9:4-5; and this showed that they were themselves affected with what they had prayed, and would not lay upon others burdens they declined to bear. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sets them in the third of the four sealing classes, following the priests. The witnesses do not divide. Together they render the Levites' place in the register as no bare formality but a meaningful step: the men who had led Israel's confession now led her in binding herself to amend, sealing as heads of their houses the covenant their own prayers had shaped. Jeshua and Binnui and Kadmiel are dim names to us, but they were the leaders of the Levitical families that carried the daily worship of the house; and that they should be found among the foremost to pledge obedience is, to the witnesses, of a piece with the whole chapter's order, in which those nearest the sanctuary are called first to the covenant, that the people might follow where their ministers had gone before.
14:
The register turns from the ministers of the house to the laity — "the chief of the people; Parosh, Pahathmoab, Elam, Zatthu, Bani" — and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the heading with care. Some of these names, he observes, are personal, some belong to families, some represent places, and some stand independent; and comparing the roll with the register of the return in Ezra 2, one sees that the intervening years had added to the number of the houses. The great clans that head the list — Parosh, Pahath-moab, Elam, Zatthu, Bani — are the very stocks that stand first among the lay houses of the return.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch reckon the chief of the people at forty-four names in all, thirteen of them traceable to the kindreds who came up with Zerubbabel; the rest are the heads of the houses into which those kindreds had divided, or the elders of the smaller towns of Benjamin and Judah. That there are forty-four here where the older list has but thirty-three they lay to the growth of the community, each kindred branching into several families whose heads all subscribed. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks that most of those named in the catalogue of Nehemiah 7:8 as heads of houses appear here among the first of the chief of the people to seal, the present head bearing the name of him who led the clan out of Babylon, and so fittest to subscribe for all his father's house.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sets these among the fourth and last class that sealed, the chief of the people filling the register from this verse to the twenty-seventh. The witnesses do not divide. What they find in the turn to the laity is the breadth of the covenant: having bound the priests and the Levites, the record now gathers in the heads of the great families, who gave it under their hands for themselves and for all the rest. Henry's word holds — those who have interest with others must use it for God — and Parosh and Elam and their fellows, named at the head of the lay roll, stand for the many households that followed their seal. The register thus moves from altar to household without a break, that the whole people, ministers and laity alike, might be seen made one in the engagement to keep the commandments of the Lord, and that no rank in Israel should be missing from the bond.
6:
The roll of sealing priests continues with Daniel, Ginnethon, and Baruch, and the witnesses treat them, as they treat the whole priestly list, less as individuals than as heads of the courses that bound themselves to the covenant. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch reckon these among the one-and-twenty priestly names set down before the summary "these were the priests," each standing for a returning course of the priesthood and subscribed here as the representative of his house. The historian, they observe, keeps the orders distinct and in their ranks, so that the record of who had pledged himself to the law might be full and exact.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the priestly names as family names rather than merely personal ones, to be compared with the register of the returning priests in Nehemiah 12:1-6; the same houses that had come up from Babylon under Zerubbabel are here found sealing the covenant a generation on. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, numbering the priests at twenty-two, marks the fitness of their leading the subscription: next after Nehemiah the governor came the priests, for those whose office it was to teach the law should be foremost in binding themselves to keep it, and their example would tell upon all the rest.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sets these names in the second of the four classes that sealed — the priests filling the verses from the second to the eighth — and joins the other witnesses in wondering that, among so many of the sacred order, neither Ezra the scribe nor the high priest Eliashib should appear. The witnesses do not divide over the bare names of Daniel and Ginnethon and Baruch; their common concern is the weight of the act these names record. Obscure as they now sound, each was a public and deliberate committal, the seal of a priestly house set to a written covenant to walk in God's law and to maintain his worship. That the reformation should be led by the priests, and that their houses should be named one by one to their lasting honour, is to the witnesses the very pattern of a right recovery — the teachers of Israel first at the sanctuary, first at the confession, and first to bind themselves before the people they were set to guide. The people who followed would see their priests pledged before them, and be the readier to pledge themselves.
12:
The register has passed from the priests to the Levites, and with Zaccur, Sherebiah, and Shebaniah it runs on through the second rank of the ministers of the house. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch count the Levites who sealed at some fourteen names, headed by Jeshua the son of Azaniah, Binnui of the sons of Henadad, and Kadmiel; the sons of Jeshua and Kadmiel, they note, had returned with seventy-four other Levites under Zerubbabel, as Nehemiah 7:43 shows, and several of these very men appear again as heads of Levitical orders in Nehemiah 12:8. Of the rest little more is known, but they are rightly regarded as heads of Levitical houses, sealing for the families they led.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds that of these Levitical family names several are traceable in the earlier lists of the return, at Ezra 2:40 and the like, so that the Levites who bind themselves here are the same stock that had first come up to rebuild the altar and the house. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, reckoning seventeen Levites in all, marks a moving thing about them: among these subscribers stood most of those who had been the mouth of the congregation in the great prayer of Nehemiah 9:4-5. This showed, he says, that they were themselves affected with what they had said, and would not bind upon others the burdens they declined to touch; those who lead in prayer should lead in every other good work.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke places these names in the third of the four sealing classes, the Levites following the priests in the verses from the ninth to the thirteenth. The witnesses do not divide over Zaccur and Sherebiah and Shebaniah; what they draw from the list is the fitness of the Levites' place in it. Set between the priests above them and the chief of the people below, the Levites who had lifted the confession of the whole nation now set their seal to the covenant that confession had prepared, sealing not for themselves alone but as heads of their houses. Henry's observation governs the reading: the men who had prayed for the people would not ask of the people what they were unwilling to promise themselves, but led in the binding as they had led in the praying. The register keeps their names, obscure as they are, that the singers of Israel's penitence might be seen among the first to pledge her amendment.
18:
With the priests and Levites sealed, the register turns to the chief of the people, and among their long roll stand Hodijah, Hashum, and Bezai. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch reckon these lay heads at forty-four names in all, of which thirteen are found in the list of the kindreds who returned with Zerubbabel in Ezra 2; the rest are either the heads of the several houses into which those kindreds had branched, or the elders of the smaller towns of Benjamin and Judah. That forty-four should appear here where only thirty-three are named in the earlier list they explain by the growth of the houses over the intervening years, each kindred having divided into several families whose heads all now subscribed.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the chief of the people in the same way: some of the names are personal, some belong to families, and some represent places, and comparing the roll with Ezra 2 one sees that the passing years had added to the number of the houses. The list is thus no random heap but a careful muster of the lay leadership of the restored community. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, numbering these chief men at forty-four, marks that they gave it under their hands for themselves and for all the rest, chiefly those over whom they had influence, that they would keep God's commandments; and their names, he says, are left upon record here to their honour, as men forward and active in reviving religion in their country — the memory of such shall be blessed.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sets these among the fourth and last class that sealed, the chiefs of the people filling the verses from the fourteenth to the twenty-seventh. The witnesses do not divide over Hodijah and Hashum and Bezai; their shared concern is the representative weight the names carry. These heads of houses subscribed not for themselves only but for the many they led, so that a whole clan was bound in the sealing of its chief. Henry's word governs the reading: those who have interest with others must use it for God, and the surest way for a great man to look great is to stand at the front of a good work. The register keeps even the obscurest of these lay names, that the honour of a covenant faithfully sealed might rest on the households they represented, and that after-ages might know at whose hands the reformation of Israel was begun, and by whose seal a whole people was held to the law of its God.
24:
Deeper into the roll of the chief of the people stand Hallohesh, Pileha, and Shobek, and the witnesses read them, like all this lay register, as the seals of representative men binding a whole people to the covenant. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch had explained that these forty-four heads of the people include both the ancient kindreds that came up with Zerubbabel and the newer houses into which those kindreds had grown; not every name answers to a family in the older list of Ezra 2, for some are the elders of the lesser towns of Judah and Benjamin, added as the community multiplied. The register, that is, reaches beyond the great clans to the local leaders of the villages, so that no part of the land should be unrepresented in the sealing.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott's rule holds over these names as over the rest: some are personal, some stand for families, and some for places, the whole list bearing the marks of a people whose houses had multiplied since the return. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry looks past the strangeness of such names to the thing they signify — that these chief men gave it under their hands, for themselves and for all whom they could sway, that they would keep the commandments of God. It is a great thing, he urges, when those who have influence over others throw it on the side of religion; and the names of Hallohesh and his fellows, dark as they now are, were once the names of men forward and active in the recovery of their nation's faith, and are set on record to their honour.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps them within the last of the four sealing classes, the chief of the people that fill out the register to its close in the twenty-seventh verse, where the final name Baanah ends the roll. The witnesses do not divide over these three obscure men; what they press is the completeness of the sealing they help to make up. Every rank has now set its hand — the governor, the priests, the Levites, and clan after clan of the laity down to the elders of the smallest towns — so that when the register ends, the whole people, through its heads, stands bound. Henry's thought presides: the leaders sealed that their example might draw the rest, and the very length of the list, running through name after forgotten name, is the measure of how broadly the covenant was owned. What a nation's chief men subscribe, a nation is held to; and here the subscription is made as wide as Israel itself, that none might afterward say the pledge was not his.
